problem: "A ray that strikes the core-cladding boundary steeper than the critical angle is reflected back inside" is ambiguous, because θc is defined from the normal to the wall but "steeper" suggests an angle measured from the wall. A student can read it backwards.
fix: "A ray that meets the core-cladding boundary at an angle to the wall normal greater than the critical angle θc is totally internally reflected and travels on."

problem: The answer says two points closer than one core diameter merge. Resolution is set by the centre-to-centre spacing of the fibres, that is core plus cladding, not the bare core diameter. This also contradicts exam trap 3, which states the spacing correctly.
fix: "Two points that fall on the same fibre, that is closer than one fibre spacing (core plus cladding, roughly 40–50 µm for a 30 µm core), merge; the 30 µm core alone is only the light-carrying part."

problem: "Air gaps between the rods keep the lens power high, so the tube stays short" gives the wrong cause. The strong refraction comes from the curved glass-air surfaces; the long glass rods help because they need fewer surfaces, so less light is lost and the relay is compact.
fix: "The curved glass-air surfaces refract strongly, and the long glass rods replace many thin lenses with fewer surfaces, so the relay loses less light and the tube can be short and bright."

where: Exam traps, bullet 2 (lamp at the tip)
problem: "The lamp stays outside the body" is stated as a general rule, but the swallowed capsule described in the same chapter carries its own tiny LEDs and battery at the tip. A student will find the two statements inconsistent.
fix: "In a conventional scope the lamp and its heat stay outside the body; only the sensor travels to the tip. The exception is the swallowed capsule, which has its own LEDs and battery inside the pill."
